title: Conflict Fix
goal: Your kids learn to fix a fight, not just end it. They cool down first, tell what happened without blame, own their own part, hear the other side, and agree on a fix, so the same argument about whose turn it is doesn't come back tomorrow.
need: A small, real fight, like whose turn it is
A separate spot for each kid to cool down
Paper for the fix, and the fridge to put it on

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is playing judge: deciding who started it and who's right. Your job is to call the cool-down, run the turns, and help them find a fix they both agree to.

plan.what: Cool down, each in their own space (Step 1).

plan.when: Same day, then a few days later
plan.what: Fix it, then check the fix (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: One of them won't let it go
troubleshoot.a: Call the cool-down again and keep them apart a little longer. Talking only works once both are ready.
Small daily fights between siblings are normal. Save the five steps for the ones that keep coming back.
Stop it right away and separate them. The talk waits until everyone is calm and safe.

lesson.text: Space and a hug can end a fight. But if nobody owns their part and nobody fixes the real problem, the same fight comes back the next day. A fix covers both: the repair between them, and the thing they were fighting about.

model.line: Each to their own space until voices are normal.
'I kept pushing your buttons.' 'I got loud and pushy.'
'You thought it was my turn for the dishes.'
Sorry, a hug, and a plan for whose turn it is.

lesson.modelNote: In our house, the space and the hug were already working. Owning each part, and fixing the dishes question itself, is what keeps the same fight from starting again tomorrow.

steps.title: Cool down
steps.why: A talk started while voices are still loud turns into round two.
steps.kid: Each kid goes to their own space until their voice is back to normal, using the Cool down card in the Conflict Fix Toolkit at the end of the guide. When they're ready, they say so.
steps.you: Say it calmly, once: 'That's enough. Each to your own space.' Then wait. Don't start the talk until both of them are calm.
ask: Are you ready to talk, or do you need more time?
steps.tip: Space first, talk second. Even five minutes apart changes the whole conversation.

levels.explore: Go to your calm spot, and come back when your voice is quiet.
levels.develop: Take space, then tell a parent when you're ready to talk.
levels.extend: Take space on your own, before anyone has to tell you to.

steps.title: Tell what happened
steps.why: Each kid has a different story. Hearing both, from the start, is the only way to get the whole picture.
steps.kid: One at a time, each kid tells what happened, using the Tell it card: the facts, one feeling word and what they wanted. No interrupting.
steps.you: Be the referee of turns, not the judge. Hand a spoon or any object to the one talking: only the one holding it speaks.
ask: What happened, from the very start?
How did you feel when that happened?
steps.tip: Ask for what they wanted, too. Under most fights, both kids wanted something fair.

levels.explore: Say what happened in one or two sentences, and one feeling.
levels.develop: Tell it from the start, with the facts, a feeling and what you wanted.
levels.extend: Tell it without one 'you always' or 'you never'.

steps.title: Own your part
steps.why: A fight takes two. When each kid names their own part, nobody has to win.
steps.kid: Each kid names one thing they did that made it bigger, using the Own it card, and says sorry for that part only.
steps.you: Go first sometimes, with a small part of your own from your day. Never make them apologize for the other kid's part.
ask: What's one thing you did that made it bigger?
What will you do differently next time?
steps.tip: 'Sorry, but you...' cancels the sorry. Own only your part, and stop there.

levels.explore: Say one thing you did, and 'I'm sorry I...'.
levels.develop: Name your part, say sorry for it, and say what you'll do next time.
levels.extend: Name your part before the other person names theirs.

steps.title: Hear their side
steps.why: Feeling heard is often what lets a kid let go, even before the problem is fixed.
steps.kid: Each kid repeats the other's side in their own words, using the Hear it card, until the other one says, 'Yes, that's it.'
steps.you: Check it out loud: 'Is that what you meant?' If not, they try again. Keep it light; it's awkward the first few times.
ask: Why might it have felt unfair to them?
steps.tip: Repeating it back feels strange at first. It's also the quickest way to stop a fight from restarting.

levels.explore: Say one thing the other person wanted.
levels.develop: Say their side back until they say 'yes, that's it'.
levels.extend: Say their side back, then say one part of it that was fair.

steps.title: Fix it, and follow through
steps.why: The hug ends the fight. The fix ends the next one.
steps.kid: Together, the kids pick a repair, like a hug or helping with the job, and a fix for the real problem, like a plan for whose turn it is. They write it in Our fix at the end of the guide, and check it a few days later.
steps.you: Help them find a fix they both say yes to, then put it where everyone sees it. A few days later, ask how it's going.
ask: What would stop this from happening again?
When should we check if the fix is working?
steps.tip: If the fix isn't working, that's not a failure. Change it together and try again.

levels.explore: Pick a way to make up, like a hug, and one idea for next time.
levels.develop: Write a fix you both agree to, and check it in a few days.
levels.extend: Write the fix, check it, and change it if it isn't working.

conclusion.headline: They know how to fix a fight, not just end it.
conclusion.text: At the next small fight, wait a moment before you step in. If one of them says 'I need space' or 'my part was...', they're using it on their own.
conclusion.celebrate: When they sort one out without you, say: 'You two fixed that on your own. That's a skill a lot of grown-ups are still working on.'
extensions: Make a family fix plan for the chore you argue about most
Work through a grown-up disagreement out loud, so they see the steps
Read a story and find each character's part in the conflict
Use the steps with a friend or teammate, not just a sibling

signs: They take space before you have to say it
They say 'my part was...' without being asked
The same fight, like whose turn it is, comes back less often
makeItReal: Pick the fight that comes back most in your house, like whose turn it is for the dishes. Once everyone is calm, sit down together, run it through the five steps, and put your fix on the fridge.

fromHome.text: My two argue every day, and they make up pretty quickly. It usually starts small, like whose turn it is to do the dishes. My daughter gets worked up, and my son keeps pushing her buttons until she gets louder, sometimes pushy, and he won't let it go. If it doesn't settle on its own, their dad or I say that's enough, and they each go their own way and take some space to calm down. Things come back to normal on their own, and they usually apologize to each other, with a hug.
